utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours, and thank you for this opportunity. I believe this is the first time that the Prosecution has requested that the Court consider an adjustment of the cross-examination allocation in advance of the witness commencing testimony. Of course, that reflects an understanding that of the Court's guiding principle which is that the allocation is not a fixed time but provided that the parties use their time efficiently and continue to inquire as to relevant issues the Court will permit a cross-examination to extend beyond the allocation assessment, and of course that also reflects the fact that it's difficult for anyone however subsumed in the minutia of the material to assess exactly how much time that will take. Nevertheless, notwithstanding that principle, in this case we wanted to address the issue in advance for two reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This case being --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In this instance with -- I'm sorry, in the instance of expert Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't make that clear from the outset. We wanted to address it in light of the convergence of both the complexity and extent of the material and -- and the actual length of the allocation, because it would, in fact, make it extremely difficult for the cross-examining lawyers to actually adjust from the material that really is critical to cover it. If I could just make a couple of small points quickly in respect of these issues and then one larger point. The two points that the Court may not have had in mind at the time would include the fact that we made a previous adjustment of time; that is, we reduced the assessment of the time we needed when we were examining Ms. Andjelkovic Lukic who also gave expert testimony, and the reason was that we understood that that expert could only speak to a few issues regarding air-bombs and that expert Subotic was the main author, notwithstanding the fact that both experts tendered that. So we already made an adjustment in connection with that, trying to be as efficient as possible, and I think clearly were during the course of that. Another factor to consider is the fact that many of the positions advanced by this expert were not put to the witnesses about whom they are now offered at the time they were here in court to deal directly with those issues or to answer such questions, and that complicates the task of the Prosecution in attempting to deal with the assertions in the Subotic reports. So that -- that is actually another interesting reflection of the wisdom of 90(h) which has not only an obvious fairness aspect but clearly has an efficiency aspect as well which effects us here. On a more general basis, although I recognise the inherent limitations of comparing one witness to another, I think it is instructive to note that the time allocated for other witnesses, so Mr. Karadzic received three hours for Witness Higgs whose report covered six scheduled incidents on mortars only and whose report was approximately 19 pages, referencing about 30 documents, and moreover, he didn't purport to do his own individual actual analysis in contrast to Witness Subotic, so that the task was significantly different. Similarly for Witness Sabljica, who as the Court will recall was a Bosnian MUP ballistics expert, he had a 74-page report covering approximately five scheduled shelling and sniping incidents, three unscheduled incidents with about 30 exhibits and the Defence received seven hours to cross-examine him. Now, in contrast this witness we are talking about three reports comprising 141 pages, 131 pages, and 151 -- 52 pages, and that's after subtracting the CVs and the redactions, and these reports comprise hundreds of documents, and the witness purports to have conducted a de novo investigation of 14 mortar, artillery and air-bomb incidents, 13 scheduled and one unscheduled. So the two lawyers focusing on this have attempted to identify as clearly as they can the most critical issues to get into, but I think -- I'm confident that the amount of time they have invested in this effort is instructive in the sense that no one casting even -- certainly not an initial review of this material much less even a -- the most intensive review that could be expected of someone who is not involved in the cross-examination could begin to appreciate the complexities involved. So with that in mind I have what I hope is a very modest proposal, Mr. President. I have talked to Ms. Gustafson and Mr. Gaynor, and I mention their names in particular because I think the Court will appreciate based on the experience in court that they are extremely skilled at using time in court efficiently, and I've asked them at the minimum additional time that would suffice under these circumstances. I would ask that the Court adjust the allocation by an additional two hours before it begins to consider whether or not additional time given the nature of the cross-examination is necessary. I think that would be a fair balance under the circumstances and permit them to at least attempt to craft their examination in a way that is not unduly difficult and that continues to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. The Chamber finds your submission to be fair enough and will grant your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue today, the Chamber will issue a decision on the Prosecution motion for testimony of Radivoje Miletic and Ljubisa Borovcanin to be viva voce, which was filed on the 2nd of May, 2013. In this motion, the Prosecution requests that the Chamber order prospective Defence witnesses Radivoje Miletic and Ljubisa Borovcanin to testify viva voce. The Prosecution submits that their positions at the time relevant to the indictment and the significant nature of their anticipated evidence concerning the Srebrenica component of the case and the criminal responsibility of the accused warrant the presentation of their evidence viva voce. The accused filed his response on the 7th of May, 2013, in which he argues that the motion should be denied. The accused submits that with regard to Borovcanin, the proposed 92 ter statement is "clear and comprehensible," the associated exhibits are limited, and he was not in proximity to the accused compared to others for whom viva voce testimony has been ordered. With respect to Miletic, the accused argues that the request is premature given that the accused's motion to subpoena him is pending and that once the Chamber grants the subpoena request it should review the potential Rule 92 ter statement before deciding whether Miletic's anticipated evidence should be led viva voce. Having reviewed the proposed Rule 92 ter statement of Borovcanin and considered his position as deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade of the VRS Ministry of Interior at the relevant time, the Chamber finds that it is appropriate to receive Borovcanin's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter as originally proposed and thus denies the Prosecution request in this respect. With regard to Miletic, the Chamber first recalls that the accused had been unsuccessful in obtaining Miletic's voluntary co-operation, and the Chamber granted the accused's motion for a subpoena. Further, having considered his proposed evidence as outlined in the accused's Rule 65 ter witness list and in the subpoena motion as well as his proximity to the accused as one of the core members of the VRS Main Staff at the relevant time, the Chamber is of the view that his evidence should be led live. Therefore, the Chamber grants the Prosecution request in relation to Miletic's testimony and orders that his evidence be led live. Unless there's anything further to be raised, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Martic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Martic. I know you just walked in. I want to make sure you're settled before I begin the questions. Then we'll commence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn next to the portion of your statement found at paragraphs 24 through 29 in which you focus for a number of paragraphs on the issue of prospective unification of the Krajinas and suggest that Mr. Karadzic resisted such unification and became more in favour of it after the war started, and again those are found in paragraphs 24 through 29, and I believe that in particular that refers to the effort in mid-1991 by persons within the Bosnian and Croatian Krajinas to unite. Now, I wanted to put to you the proposition that the opposition to the unification of the Bosnian and Croatian Krajina at that time did not reflect an opposition to unification -- to the concept of the unification of all Serbs in one state generally but arose instead out of a tactical concern, a concern that the time was not right for doing so, that to do so at that moment would result in less territory for the Serbs and that it would be done when the time was right, after, for example, proposed agreements had been rejected by the other side. That's -- that's the nature of the opposition to the unification of the Krajinas in mid-1991 that is discussed in paragraphs 24 through 29 of your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you interpreted all that in your own way, and it does not tally with the truth, not absolutely. If you're interested in my view of the thing, of course I will share it with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you some specific questions and perhaps we can identify the extent to which it corresponds with what happened at the time and any nuances or larger issues in which you claim it does not. This Trial Chamber, for example, has received evidence, that's P2555, that Dr. Karadzic was concerned that if the Krajinas united at that time, it would be viewed as a kind of secession from Bosnia by the Serbs and the Serbs would only end up with half the territory that he considered they should have. Were you aware of that at the time, that that was his position on the issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. This does not reflect the truth, and I have to explain. The attention of unification and declaration of unification that was issued on the 27th of June in Grahovo, if I remember it well, and that was issued by the SAO Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina, happened after both Croatia and Slovenia declared their independence and secession from Yugoslavia. Milan Babic as the creator of that unification was an undisputable authority not only in our Krajina but also in that part. He initiated the unification --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, I'm sorry, and again I'm glad we had the brief discussion the other day about the need to focus on the question. My question is not the backdrop to the unification or who was primarily responsible for moving it forward. Your statement focuses on Dr. Karadzic's opposition to the unification in those paragraphs. I put to you that his unification was grounded not on an opposition to the concept of all Serbs in one state generally but because the timing wasn't right and it would result in this -- and a unification at that time would result in less territory for the Serbs than was desired. And I asked you if you were familiar with his position on that as reflected in a telephone conversation which this Court has received in evidence at P2555.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say again this does not reflect the situation as it was during that period of time. Dr. Karadzic exclusively advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia, and that is the truth. He was not in favour of a Serbian territory but, rather, the preservation of Yugoslavia. The unification, as I understood it, would result in the destruction of our idea to preserve Yugoslavia. That moment he was far-sighted, and he saw more than the rest of us who were in favour of the unification. He was concerned about the preservation of Yugoslavia and the destruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If that declaration was not -- had not been annulled on that same day, they would have put us in the same position as Milan Babic. And let me repeat. This does not apply to what you say, the Serbian territory and that Serbs would have gained less. It was all about the preservation of Yugoslavia. That was all it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not the preservation of Yugoslavia in its existing composition. You were aware, were you not, that Dr. Karadzic was speaking before the commencement of the conflict about the effort to concern about desire to keep the Serbian portions of Bosnia within Yugoslavia so that then the Bosnian Serb -- the Serbian leadership would have provided the Krajinas with a link to Yugoslavia, that is, with the Serbian countries, the future state; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Dr. Karadzic and the majority of the leading people in Yugoslavia and Serbia fought hard for the preservation of Yugoslavia. There were talks about our rights based on the constitution and the constitution gave equal rights to Serbs, Croats and others, the right to self-determination if it was impossible to go on living together. I'm not excluding that possibility either. There were talks about the other republics, i.e., the other peoples, and if they continued insisting on separatism, we thought that we should use that right, the right of self-determination and making a decision who we would live with if they wanted to leave Yugoslavia, and I mean Croats, Slovenes and others, they could but only pursuant to the constitution. And in that respect I can understand Karadzic's word, if he indeed used them, that us Serbs should also consider our options provided by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you say of course not, but then you go on to explain that that seems to be -- that the proposition I put to you indeed seems to be correct or at least you accept that it could be correct; is that right? Or do you -- I just need to know where you stand on this thing. Do you say: That was not Dr. Karadzic's position and I know that's the case, or, yes, that may have been Dr. Karadzic's position to make sure the Serbian leadership kept what they considered to be the Serbian parts of Bosnia linked to the other Serbian parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're presenting things the way you want, and you're not analysing Dr. Karadzic's words properly. I repeat for an umpteenth time that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic, the president of the then Presidency, advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia. They stuck to the constitution, and the constitution gave the rights to the peoples, not the republics, the peoples, the right to self-determination to cessation. This is what it was all about. There was -- that was not about a plan to create a Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's not jump ahead, Mr. Martic. Let's just stick to the concrete discussions that did or did not take place. So in December of 1991 isn't it true that Dr. Karadzic was already talking about the benefit of managing to keep what Serbian leaders considered the Serbian parts, the Serbian areas of Bosnia, linked to the other Serbian parts of former Yugoslavia? That's all. Isn't that what Dr. Karadzic was in fact talking about in December of 1991, well before the commencement of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was saying in December. I don't know. I can't see that. But I know from my several encounters with Dr. Karadzic and from his several debates that Serbs had to adhere to the constitution. As far as the fact that Serbian territories are interconnected in many parts, I'm sure that you can't blame Dr. Karadzic for that. This is a fact that preexisted that situation; for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in cadastral terms, the Serbs had over 60 per cent of the territory where they resided. This is not a figment of Mr. Karadzic's imagination. Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, the -- the -- regardless of the nuances of what you assert Dr. Karadzic was -- was or was not saying at the time, and this Court has received evidence in respect of those issues, for example, the December 1991 meeting I just referred to as P25554 and the particular comment that I referred to is found - this is for the benefit of the parties - at the e-court English page 49 and B/C/S page 68, the reality is that the leadership of the Serbian people in Bosnia, in Croatia, and in Serbia held as a long-term objective the state unity of the Serbs, all Serbs in one state; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way you make up this construct, Serbs in one state, but that's a reference to Yugoslavia. That Yugoslavia, let me remind you, was established by the Serbs, and they made it possible for other nations to live in that state as well, and that through two world wars, and that kind of Yugoslavia was acceptable to the Serbs, and we thought that it was acceptable to others, too, but it turned out that apparently it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So is it your position in this Court, Mr. Martic, that once it became apparent that Yugoslavia was dissolving and would exist no more that the Bosnian Serbs, the Croatian Serbs, and the Serbian leadership in Belgrade decided that it was no longer a goal or objective that all Serbs should be within the same state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all let me state this: Yugoslavia did not fall apart, and it wasn't dissolving or falling apart. It is broken up from the outside especially by the Vatican and the Germans. It was smashed, deconstructed. And in this destruction we as a constituent nation, not only in Serbia but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, thought of how we could remain and live together. The right to self-determination that was given to other nations, we were entitled to that, weren't we? I don't know what else you want me to say. Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I wanted you to answer the question which I'm not sure was answered, so let me try it in a slightly different way. I mentioned the leaderships in Bosnia, the leadership in Croatia, the leadership in Belgrade, so let me show you three documents, one emanating from each of those entities and ask you again about the objective of ensuring that all Serbs were in one state. So if we could first call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Can I intervene at the moment. Mr. Martic, a minute ago you said you -- "We could remain and live together." Who are "we"? Did you mean the Serbs as a constituent people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs as a constituent nation including other nations, Slovenes, Croats, Muslims, Macedonians, and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency, that's exactly what I wanted to intervene in transcript, because "we as a constituent nation" not only in Serbia but in all Yugoslavia, Bosnia, this constituent didn't -- hadn't been reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we call up first P748.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document already in evidence, so I can begin noting for you what it contains. This is a -- I'm sorry, instead I'd like 65 ter 06618. I think that would be more efficient. I was first going to call up one emanating from the Bosnian Serb leadership, and this is a document dated the 19th of December, 1991, a date I imagine you remember, and it's sent by Mr. Krajisnik referring to the historic occasion of the proclamation of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina as the Republic of Serbian Krajina as the RSK. He indicates: "I am unable to join you on the verification of the historical right of the Serbian people to live in one state." He requests that his whole-hearted congratulations be conveyed, and he continues later in the document, in the middle of the document, all Serbs are engaged in a struggle for the same goal under the same banner and we are all convinced of our ultimate victory. I could also turn next to 65 ter 25048. This is a document emanating from Belgrade, specifically from Mr. Stanisic. Sorry, there seems to be a potential concern about the number, which there may be -- let me check on that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's not a bad idea to pull up document by document --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and present it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, yeah. I wanted to be as efficient as possible. These are all documents dealing with exactly the same issue coming from different places and different relevant places. Okay. That was the previous document we saw. Sorry, if you didn't have it in front of you at the time I'm sorry, and you can see the references that I made in court are found in the first paragraph, the second paragraph, and the fourth paragraph, as well as you can see in the third paragraph a reference to not dividing us into several states. And if we could turn next -- okay, that's 65 ter 25051. That was the problem. Can we turn next to 25048. As you can see here, Mr. Martic, this is a document from the previous -- the previous document on the screen was exactly right. I don't know where it just went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you want 25051. 25048 is a 1994 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Anyway if the previous document is 25051, that's the one we want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, I was starting to explain that was a document from Mr. Stanisic, the head of the state security department of the Republic of Serbia MUP, and he's writing on the occasion of security day of the republic of RSK and notes that we are now entering the decisive phase of the fight to achieve the common goals of all the Serbian lands more determined and prepared than ever before. And finally I indicated I would show you in addition documents emanating from Croatian -- the Croatian Serbian leadership, and that's 65 ter 25045. Now, I imagine you recognise these documents, Mr. Martic. These are holiday greeting cards sent to Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, to Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and also to Momcilo Perisic, indicating that the previous year had been characterised by efforts to achieve united news towards a common goal, the creation of a united Serbian state and expressing the hope that in the upcoming year you will all be working together toward the same goals and sending cordial wishes. Now, Mr. Martic, I showed you all those because I wanted to put to you the fact that the unification of the Serbs, the creation of a united Serb state, was a goal shared by the leaderships of the Croatian Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, and the Serbs in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is your interpretation, but I observe one thing here: Everything that you have said has to do with various periods. The first one was from 1991, and the other two documents, the other two events or whatever was shown here, was -- were from 1994 and even 1995. There is a huge difference in the interpretation of what you have said. In this event where the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, extends his congratulations has to do with our declaration of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina which was declared at the moment when it was already known that Croatia would be recognised by the international community and that peacekeeping forces would come to our territories where they would be a protection force, and as for the political solution for that part, the Krajina, that that would be undertaken by peaceful means --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, excuse me. I -- we -- I don't object in theory to the most expansive answers. We just don't have the time for you to provide the backdrop to every issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tieger, in this case I think it's better to hear him out. Please continue, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the other two instances, after three and even four years, many things had happened in the meantime. At this time there were several aggressions taken against the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, and practically the Vance Plan had already been destroyed. At that time war was raging in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After many events, thorough attempts to do this peacefully the international community did not allow this. They agreed and condoned the separatism of Slovenia and Croatia and even they recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, although they were aware themselves that it would lead to war. As the situation evolved in 1994 and 1994 [as interpreted], it was quite normal that we, too, would think about unity and unification of the remaining territories, which was the Republic of Serbia, Montenegro, the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska, that we should unite and live together. And again this was within the framework of the constitution that all the nations, and we were a constituent nation both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, that we would be entitled to self-determination. So everything arose from that, because there was not a single reason why the international community would not recognise and respect for us the same right that they had recognised for others. Unfortunately, this unification never materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn in a moment to some of the steps taken in pursuit of the goal that I've focused on, but first I want to tender those three documents and then I want to ask you another question about the judgement in your trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll permit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 06618 will be Exhibit P6306, 65 ter number 25051 will be Exhibit P6307, and 65 ter number 25045 will be Exhibit P6308.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, your Trial Chamber found: "The evidence establishes the existence as of early 1991 of a political objective to unite Serb areas in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina with Serbia in order to establish a unified territory." Do you dispute that that was their finding at paragraph 442, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to be shown that paragraph if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 25046, and as I say paragraph 442.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but could I see the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English version before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not say paragraph 442?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you have is 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. That's why I mentioned it again. I thought there had been an adjustment made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: E-court page 159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I am reading from the second sentence: "The evidence establishes the existence as of early 1991 of a political objective to unite Serb areas of Croatia and in Bosnia with Serbia in order to establish a unified territory." Now, you can confirm it or not? I'm going to -- we can -- we can refer to it in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we're here, what does section III I deal with? I am seeing the footnote. I will leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So what section -- section III is factual findings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't know at moment what -- we don't know what evidence it does refer to, but you may put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes or no, Mr. Martic? I don't want to spend too much time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if he can't read it, I don't understand how he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he remembers what Mr. Tieger read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's unfortunate, because if you look a few sentences down you'll see that this is qualifying the fact that it was not -- did not itself amount to a common purpose. So it's somewhat misleading to just show it -- to just read one sentence to the witness without him being able to see the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then it goes on -- it goes on to talk about the implementation through the commission of crimes which were found in -- in the -- in this particular case and in this particular judgement. We are talking about the objective. I focused on that objective alone, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tieger, instead of relying on the judgement, what -- could you not just simply put your case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I intended to rely on both. All right. Very quickly, Mr. Martic, let me ask you another question and I'll move on to something else. That objective was also reflected in documents referring to and justifying and explaining military operations, correct, such as Operation Corridor; that is the objective of uniting the Serbs, linking the Krajinas to the mother country, et cetera. Was cited in military documents and other documents referring to Operation Corridor, including documents by yourself. Would you like to see one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 25047, please. This is a document you sent to the committee to mark the anniversary of the liberation of Cer. That was one the early places "liberated" during Operation Corridor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you stated there opening a corridor to Serbia through your beautiful area was not only a great military victory, it was also a merging of the Serbian Krajinas with the motherland Serbian: "Dear brethren and comrades in arms, we hope that this route will not only be successfully defended and preserved but that it will be extended so that after the unification of the RS and the RSK making use of our joint victory at the corridor we shall finally also be united with our brethren in Serbia and Montenegro." Now, that's another expression this time by you although there are other military documents reflect similar sentiments about the objective of uniting Serb -- what was considered to be Serb lands and uniting the Serb people in one state.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if you could answer yes or no and then if you need to explain it go ahead, but I'd like to know where you stand on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that requires an explanation. I cannot answer with a simple yes or no. When we look at this document that I sent, it's -- it was already in 1995, on the 14th of June. So we are going back to the period when all the possibilities were exhausted for us --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to gain the right on the basis of the constitution -- do you want me to talk about the corridor or what is it that you want to hear from me? In any case, our aspirations were indeed to determine who we were going to live with. If everyone else was given the right, both the Slovenes and the Croats and the Macedonians, why then would we be the only ones who could not self-determine ourselves in a legitimate way, which was provided by the constitution of the SFRY and the republic in which we lived. But if you would like me to explain about this famous corridor and to say a few words about it no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We may address that, but right now first of all I tender this document Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But right now I want to move on to the issue of some of the concrete assistance that Serbia provided in support of the effort -- efforts of the Croatian Serbs and the Bosnian Serbs to unite. And if we could turn first to P4263. That would be clip 1. Let me explain it by way of background. This Court has received evidence already concerning a ceremony that was held in Serbia in 1997 to mark the anniversary of the formation of the special operations unit of the State Security Service, and I wanted to turn to some aspects of that if we can, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is a portion of the ceremony in which Dragan Vasiljkovic is recognised. In this case he's embraced by another man. Perhaps you can identify both people here. Do you recognise the man -- well, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the man on the right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the man on the right is Jovica Stanisic. The man on the left is Dragan Vasiljkovic, Captain Dragan, and that's found at 43:29.9. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to turn to the -- let's turn to clip 3 of -- quickly to 42 - 45235A. Oh, I'm sorry, P2852. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And stop. Do you recognise the man in the red beret?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Legija, Ulemek. Milorad Ulemek.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he was Arkan's deputy, is that right, and was an instructor at the Erdut training centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was an instructor at Erdut is not something I know. I know that he was in Arkan's units, and as far as I know, at the final stage he joined the units of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next to 42 -- P4263, clip 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask Mr. Tieger to tell us what year this is. Can we have the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I announced it at the beginning. This document is already in evidence. I believe it's 1997. By the way, I spoke with Mr. Robinson before we began about the problem of clips in a document like this. Virtually the entirety of the speech that I'm going to turn to next is in evidence as one of the clips but not a particular portion that I wanted to refer to, and so it's sometimes a little more cumbersome to have portions of documents than -- especially when large numbers of them are incorporated as others. Okay. We turn next to 4 -- 65 ter 45235D, which has the entirety of the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. President, we thank you for accepting the invitation to attend the ceremony marking the anniversary of the formation of the special operations unit of the State Security Service. It was constituted on the 4th of May, 1991, at the time of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, and since it emerged has constantly worked to protect national security in the circumstances where the existence of the Serbian people was directly jeopardised through its entire ethnic area. Its combat operations were anti-terrorist directed at preventing war crimes, mass retaliation, and genocide. From the first moment of its existence and establishment, the unit has passed through a heroic epic and its part has been one of the most difficult ones in the history of our struggle. Due to the international circumstances familiar to us all, we were forced to operate in complete secrecy."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, did you recognise the speaker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Franko Simatovic, Frenki, who's speaking. But the image that I'm seeing, that you're showing me, is that of President Milosevic, Jovica Stanisic, and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And that's -- that's -- the last comment of the witness's is a reference to where we stopped at 13:28.3. Now, much of this speech is in evidence, and Mr. Simatovic goes on to explain about the unit's history. Mr. President, allow us to inform you briefly about the unit's history, its combat record, present situation and function, and he states: "When it was formed, its corps was made up of members of our service, Republic of Serbian Krajina police, and volunteers from Serbia." He then goes on to talk about various battles with armed Croatian police forces in different areas, and he talks about the establishment of 26 training camps for Special Police Units of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina: "26 training camps for Special Police Units of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were also formed in that period. In the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Golubic, Dinara, Obrovac, Gracac, Plitvice, Sumarice," and so on and so on, "including ending with Ilok and Vukovar." And then he states it's written in RSK but it appears to be a reference in RS, in Banja Luka, Doboj, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, and other places. And then for benefit of the parties that's found at page 11 of the transcript. The previous references were at page 10 of the transcript. And finally two other references I want to bring your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Page 11 of what? What transcript, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the transcript of the entirety of the video that was taken at Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we have is only four pages in the number you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. Right. I'm sorry, no reference is needed there. This is a reference to the fact that I thought it would be far more efficient at this point to tender this entire exhibits since I'm going to be referring -- this is -- this is the transcript of the current 65 ter number on the screen, 45235, which is the -- should be the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you not say 45 -- I'm sorry. 45235B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. President. I called out the clip of the Simatovic speech. I think we can certainly call up the entirety, which is 45235, and that might be a much easier way to work over the long haul. In any event, in one way or another I'm still referring to the speech by Mr. Simatovic. So I can -- the parties can follow in the current variation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic goes on to note, Mr. Martic, that the centre -- "The centre in which we are now bears the name of Radislav Kostic, a distinguished member of this unit who was killed three years ago in western," and that part can't be heard. And then he goes on to describe when the service took over the building and how it transformed it into a modern centre with training grounds, firing range, heliport, and so on. And you were -- you were familiar with Mr. Kostic; correct? You knew him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, shortly after Mr. Simatovic concludes his speech, there is a moment when Mr. Simatovic pauses and says: "Mr. President, dear guests, let us pay tribute to deputy minister Radovan Stojicic, Badza, by observing a minute of silence," and that is done. And again, I take it you were familiar with Mr. Stojicic also known as Badza; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with reference to the training camps that were referred to by Mr. Simatovic, the first one he mentions is Golubic, and you -- you were familiar with that particular training camp; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was. I established it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the references to training camps at Ilok and Vukovar, those camps are not referred to by name, but is it -- is it correct that the reference to Vukovar is a reference to the Erdut camp and the reference to Ilok is a reference to the Pajzos camp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume so, though of course there's a difference and quite a big difference as to who had -- who was in charge of these camps and at what periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When we have occasion to make reference to any of those camps specifically, you can indicate what you think is appropriate by way of that particular time for who was in charge at that moment. Now, in collection with Golubic, let's take a look at another video. That's 65 ter 40060A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may be obvious to everyone in the courtroom, but for the record we should indicate this is you in front of the troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at some sort of review at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we happened to stop it at 41.7. If we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, it's obvious but if you can identify the people in the foreground.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first on the left is General Ratko Mladic; Sejdo Bajramovic is in the middle, he was a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia at the time; and Jugoslav Kostic, also a member of the Yugoslav Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can continue. That's at 1:35.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16, it's not "Cedo Bajramovic," it's "Sejdo Bajramovic," which again in our parts indicates the religious affiliation and ethnicity. Sejdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next clip, please. Next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is Arkan; correct? Zeljko Raznjatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's at 3:39.9. The next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that was you again at the portion preceding 3:51? Correct, Mr. Martic? That was you speaking again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you able to hear your words, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not, but I can see that I was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tieger, is it your plan that you play this video without sound? I take it there's a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is a transcript, and I think it was provided, but if not, I apologise for that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tieger repeat the reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. It's 65 ter 40060A, and this appears at the first page. I think there's only one page provided.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have it. Yes, we have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we play where Mr. Milan Martic said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Milan Martic: Dear guests of this ceremony for all the soldiers who fell for our Krajina, may they rest in eternal glory. "Zeljko Raznatovic: Against the Ustashas, about the defence against the dagger, about the defence of the Serbian people not only in the Krajina but throughout our blood drenched Serbian land because us must know that this has never been a part of Croatia. The Serbian people paid for this land with blood. I say to you that this never belonged to Croatia. This is Serbia and will always be a part of the Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, I -- I -- I tender those clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those clips being ... this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This one and the previous clips we saw beginning with Mr. Martic reviewing the troops. That's 40060A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, Mr. President. Can we know the dates of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This document has to be contextually dated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, can you provide the date on which this ceremony took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This ceremony was held, I believe, in the spring, April, perhaps even earlier in 1992, after a certain sort of truce was achieved and the forces of the United Nations began deploying in our area. The event itself has to do with the inauguration of an education centre where personnel was to be trained, and this is why the people were present. You didn't play my speech, but that's exactly the point I'm making, that we want to have educated and trained cadre that would work professionally and in accordance with the law, and as for what you're saying, that there were other people present and saying certain things, I don't see anything bad in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can admit it in one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we're sign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6310, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask something? Was the bit that Mr. Martic said and that wasn't played to us now transcribed? Do we have this in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that has been transcribed, just a line. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's referring to the rest of what Mr. Martic said and a part that wasn't on the video but on the same occasion. I think he's asking whether there's a transcript of that that we might use in redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, there is not to my knowledge, although the defence of course has the entire tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, I wanted to turn back to what Mr. Simatovic was talking about in the ceremony at Kula in Serbia, and that is about the three arms of the unit, the special unit, and he mentioned, as we discussed before, the DB, the RSK, police, and volunteers. So let me turn first to the issue of the State Security Service of the republic -- under the Serbian MP. Now, Simatovic also mentioned the name of Rade Kostic for whom the centre was named as a distinguished member of the unit and distinguished -- the language is -- right, well, distinguished member of this unit who was killed three years ago. Now, you also knew Mr. Kostic, is it correct, as, among other things, someone who became an assistant member -- assistant minister in the MUP of the RSK, that is in the police of the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a friend of mine and my assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if just we could call up 65 ter 25048 quickly. This reflects the minutes of a board meeting of the MUP on the 10th of June, 1994, and I call it to your attention simply because it indicates that Mr. Kostic and Ilija Kojic are assistant ministers of the RSK movement. That's at the top of the page. And I take it you can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to being an assistant minister in the MUP, Mr. Kostic, as indicated in the Kula video, was also a member of the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And his superior was Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the same was true of Mr. Kojic as well. He was also a member of the State Security Service whose superior was Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, with one difference. I asked these people to assist me, and I was provided with Kojic and Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were aware that Mr. Stanic's superior was Mr. Milosevic himself; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to some sort of structure that should be the case, though I never looked in detail into their rules and who their supervisor was. I think the situation there was a bit complex. At any rate, you could tell -- you could say that their boss was the then president of the Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the then President of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, you indicate in a portion of your statement -- let me find it quickly. Paragraph 43, that you had no contact with Milosevic and did not report directly or indirectly to him. Now, you mentioned time periods a couple of times during your testimony. Is that a reference to a particular time period or does that mean that throughout the course of the conflict, meaning from 1991 through 1995, you did not have contact with Milosevic and did not report directly or indirectly to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. The statement actually doesn't say anything about having -- he's never said he didn't have contact with Milosevic. I think that makes it erroneous. It says, "I did not report directly or indirectly to Slobodan Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, I appreciate the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But, excuse me, I had it written down. I thought Mr. Robinson was actually correcting it accurately. In fact, it states: "I did not report directly or indirectly to Slobodan Milosevic. No incidents were manufactured by Slobodan Milosevic. In fact, during this period I had no contact with Slobodan Milosevic." So I renew my question to you, Mr. Martic, because you've been -- on a couple of occasions you've sought to refer to particular times during the course of the war. I ask you, does this refer to some particular time, or does it reflect the -- your position about your -- the nature of your contact and relationship with Mr. Milosevic from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about a specific period, specifically 1990 through to the autumn of 1991. In that period, I never personally saw Mr. Milosevic and had almost no contact with him. All of this was stated in the context of the statements by Milan Babic who invented some sort of parallel structures and about how Slobodan Milosevic engineered conflicts in our area, and this didn't have a shred of truth in it. He invented the parallel structures and the influence of the Security Service of Serbia and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, we're discussing that. This is not an occasion for you to repeat the allegations in your statement but to respond to the questions. That question was about the time period we're talking about. So in that respect, then, I take it -- does that mean you later had contact with Mr. Milosevic and does that mean that you later reported directly or indirectly to Mr. Milosevic, that is after the time period you just identified?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did have contact, but your second question about me reporting to him or being answerable to him, that's -- that something -- that really doesn't stand. A co-operation is one thing, and me being answerable to him or him issuing orders to me is quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an appropriate time to take the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm afraid there's a bit of misunderstanding coming out from translation. "Reporting" and "odgovarao," and responding or being subjugated, and President Martic said that the other part was not right. He was not superior to President Martic. Because Mr. Tieger said reporting, but translation that came to President Martic was "odgovarao," [interpretation] being answerable, [In English], being responsible to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President. That was what I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, before we -- just before we adjourned, you were talking about the nature of your contact and relationship with Mr. Milosevic, and you stated that you did have contact but that as far as you reporting to him or being answerable to him, that doesn't stand having co-operation and issuing orders. Having co-operation is one thing. Issuing orders is quite a different matter. In that connection I'd like to look at two documents. The first is 65 ter 01 -- 08160. This document is dated the 7th of December, 1994. It's from the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and it states -- it's headed "To the president of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, Mr. Milan Martic, and the commander of the Main Staff of the SVK, the Serbian Krajina, Major Celeketic," and is that states: "On the order of the president of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, urgently facilitate the passage of UNPROFOR humanitarian aid in Western Bosnia ..." And it explains the reasons, the first of which is that you, Mr. Martic, promised this to Mr. Akashi, and it provides that a report should be submitted on the completed task to the President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic, by tomorrow at 0800 hours. Now, this document, Mr. Martic, is a reflection of an order that you and Mr. Celeketic received from Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can treat this as an order but this is not an order. If you will allow me, I will explain what this is about. The convoys in question requested by Mr. Akashi and the Red Cross were sent to the forces of the 5th Corps in the Cazin and Bihac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic. Mr. Martic, I have limited time. If it's necessary to explain the backdrop to what is explicitly identified as an order and that explicitly instructs you to submit a report on the completed task, then you -- the Court will permit you to do so, but if you want to -- if you're explaining the backdrop to this order and how this order came about, that's not something that we're interested in at the moment. I'm just focusing on the fact that on the 7th of December, 1994, Mr. Milosevic issued an order to you, and I will follow up with your response.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is how it is written, but the wording may be a bit awkward. I know that President Milosevic was often served incorrect information. Maybe that was conveyed to him, and those who were in charge in the General Staff conveyed his instruction to me in the form of an order. I did not consider this to be an order. It was just my obligation to, firstly, deal with the misunderstanding and involve the Red Cross and to eliminate it, and that was the only time that we had prevented the passage of convoys. Before that and a hundred time after that the convoys were allowed to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question -- I'm not getting into the subject of convoys and humanitarian assistance for this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the explanation is important. It is important to know how the misunderstanding arose, but if the Prosecutor is not interested, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You made it clear that you didn't consider this to be an order. That's sufficient for our purpose. We'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6312, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the fact of the matter is that there was an immediate response on the same day to that order, which was explicitly identified as an order, and it also refers to the document as order and if we could turn to 65 ter 25034. 25034. This is a document dated the very same day. It's signed and stamped, signed by General Celeketic. It's sent to Mr. Milosevic, identified as Mr. President, and states "As regards to your order sent by telegram," et cetera, et cetera, "we inform you that we carried out your order," and explains how that was done. So it's correct, is it not, Mr. Martic, that this is -- this is the fulfillment of the requirement of the previous document that you and General Celeketic report back by 0800 hours of the following morning, and it against refers to the previous document as an order; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. However, I have to add to this that this is more an expression of respect towards President Milosevic, and that's why the word "order" was used. Maybe I can explain. According to this hierarchy line, when General Celeketic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, I'm -- if the Court wants you to explain, that's fine. If Mr. Karadzic wants you to explain also during his redirect he can ask for further elaboration, but it seems to me that you provided the nature of the same answer that you did before, which is that this is -- that you explained why -- your view of why the term order was used and I wasn't asking for a general hierarchy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked whether this was an order and the witness disagreed and wanted to explain his -- explain why he didn't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that it was an order. It may be fair enough to hear his explanation, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Martic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we can read in here is more an expression of courtesy or respect for President Milosevic. However, in reality, General Celeketic, when he was introduced to President Milosevic after having been appointed commander of the forces of the Army of Republic of Serbian Krajina said literally, "President Milosevic, I respect you however the only person who can give me orders and the only orders I am going to carry out will come from my President, Mr. Martic," and that's what President Milosevic took into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 25034, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation. The interpretation into English was not good. It says here -- or, rather, the translation is not good. It says here, "as regards to your order on my obligation." [In English] Carried out the obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Then, Mr. Martic, could you read out the first sentence. Read aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Mr. President, as regards of your order sent by the telegram of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, confidential number 1488-1 dated 7 December 1994, we inform you that we have carried out your order."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the title of the document. The type of this document is defined by the title which you can find below the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We see that. It's a subject you can take up in your re-examination if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Exactly. That's not an appropriate intervention in -- in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought it was a translation issue of the first sentence. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But by -- although we have completed this issue. How is this issue whether -- i.e., whether it is an order or not, is relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because this is -- because it's relevant to this witness's credibility. It's not an independent -- necessarily an independent issue in the first place. Secondly, Mr. President, we're seeing the appearance of numerous people for the same purpose doing the relatively same tasks in both places, and of course that's relevant to the -- to command and control, the JCE, and so on. So it has -- it's relevant for both reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I lost track of the transcript to see if that was admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, you earlier explained that Mr. Kostic and Mr. Kojic were members of the DB for whom Jovica Stanisic was their superior. It's correct, isn't it, that at some point you had a conflict with Mr. Kostic and Mr. Kojic and one that -- and turned to Mr. Milosevic for assistance in that regard; right? I'm referring to being stopped at the border in October of 1994. You remember that; right? Do you want me to show you the document that emanated from that episode?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember, but I have to say that prior to that both Kostic and Kojic were members of the MUP of Croatia. The MUP of Croatia expelled them like it did all the other Serbs. They were temporarily members of the DB. At my request they were assigned to me. I believe that this is very important. And as for your question, I can say that we did have a conflict, and what you stated in your question is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, they were -- after they were no longer in the MUP of Croatia, in the very early stages of events you requested their assistance for your MUP and then later on there came the time of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just show you two documents quickly, if I may, that reflect those events. The first is 65 ter 05343. I'm just going to move through that document fairly quickly, sir. If we could turn to the next page, that's right. This is as we see a document dated the 7th of October. It's you writing to Mr. Milosevic and others regarding an incident at the Tovarnik crossing and you explain at the beginning how you were crossing on October 4th, that we're told as you were to cross that the crossing on the RSK side was under the control of Ilija Kojic's men. You go on to describe how you were stopped at gunpoint and the cars searched. You then explain who you consider to be responsible for it as you indicate in the middle of the paragraph at page 3 in the English, the men who organised the incident were members of the paramilitary and parapolice forces stationed in Erdut. They were under the direct control of Rade Kostic of the state security department, and so on. And then as we see at the back of the page you seek Mr. Milosevic's -- or toward the back, seek his assistance and indicate to him that you would consider -- at the moment you would not go public with that information but would consider various steps if that didn't happen -- if this matter wasn't addressed. So that was the letter sent on the 7th of October, and similarly in terms of efficiency -- first of all, you remember sending that letter, I take it; right? That concerns the incident at that we eluded to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's also correct that immediately after the incident on that same day of October 4th, you were upset about what happened. You telephoned Mr. Milosevic and essentially related the same thing, explained to him what had happened to you at the crossing, who you considered responsible, and asked him to deal with it by ordering Mr. Stanic to withdraw those people. And let me give you some help with that. Let's turn to 32810. So again, Mr. Martic, as I explained a moment ago, this is a record of a telephone conversation between you and Mr. Milosevic, an intercepted telephone conversation dated the 4th of October, 1994, and as you can see at the beginning, you indicate you're calling from Vukovar. You just got the shock of your life. It was really intolerable. And you explained that the same gang make arrested before. They came from Erdut, they waited for you, held you at gunpoint, searched every vehicle, and so on, and then you go on repeatedly during the course of that conversation to insist that Mr. Milosevic ordered Stanic to withdraw that -- that -- the people involved. So I just wanted you to confirm that that's a reflection of the telephone conversation that you had immediately after these events that preceded the letter you sent on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is all correct. Maybe this calls for an elaboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not -- I -- I think it's fairly straightforward. I am interested in moving on. I am -- the Court may have a different view. I'm not trying to unfairly limit your testimony, sir, but my -- I think the questions I had about this document have been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, can I ask you the -- about the relevance to Mr. Karadzic's case of this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. The incident itself is not relevant by -- first of all, I'm a little reluctant to answer in front of the witness. Normally I would approach the Bench on a matter like this. So if I'm more elliptical than I would like to be I hope the Court will understand. The Court has already -- the structure of the special unit, including members of the DB, volunteers, RSK police and so on, has already been raised. I spent some time identifying the overall objective and then started to look at the steps that were introduced to -- by the participants in those events, by in this case the Republic of Serbia, to further those efforts. We've seen any number of the same figures operating in Bosnia, and I'm going to in a moment, I hope, ask a couple of questions about -- about Arkan, about Captain Dragan that reflect that, and I've already asked about Mr. Kostic whose position is reflected in this document. This Court has already received evidence about Mr. Kostic in connection with events in Zvornik. So there it's a great deal of inter-connection. This helps illuminate the connections between the people involved on the ground in events in Bosnia and other figures in Belgrade, other figures throughout the territories that were claimed by the Serbs in an effort to unify the territories considered to be Serb. So I -- again, when you're seeing familiar names, knowing what their hierarchical relationship is to others who share objectives, knowing when they were sent and why they were sent, I submit, is extremely relevant for the Court's consideration of how they ended up in various parts of Bosnia and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any objection to the admission of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits 6314 and 6315 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, similarly I had a brief discussion with Mr. Robinson at the break concerning the Kula video, and I'm pleased that he agreed with the assessment that given the number of references to that video and the material already in evidence, that it would be sound to tender the entirety of that video, and I would do so now. That's 45235. I think I indicated I had an intention of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was not shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He say various parts of it, Mr. President, including parts that are already in evidence and he heard references to other parts. So I -- and we discussed various aspects of what transpired at that event. So he saw -- sorry, perhaps if I had done it at the time it would have been clearer to the Court but we saw quite a number of parts including Mr. Simatovic's speech. We saw Legija, we saw Captain Dragan, we heard references to Badza and Mr. Kostic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, was this witness present at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think our position would be different then. I didn't realise that. I think if the witness was present, we wouldn't have any objection, but if he wasn't present, then we think it should be limited to those portions that he can comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, my point was he commented on so much of the -- of the video that the continued practice of simply admitting excerpts I think is creating more awkwardness and confusion than necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my memory's correct that you made a reference certain part of the video-clip, and you asked about the specific individual, which Mr. Martic confirmed. We'll come back to this issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. Okay. Mr. President, by the way, I think I'm nearly at my two hours. I have -- I want to cover just a few more documents in relation to people we've already discussed. I have dramatically reduced even before we began but certainly since we began given the length of the responses the amount of material I want to cover, but I have three very specific areas I'd like to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And which will take how long, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm hoping no more than a half an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Normally we don't take a position on these things, but in this case I think we would object to an extension of the time because, first of all, the witness's answers have been very brief. This is not a witness who has gone on and on, and Mr. Tieger made some choices about topics that you yourself have questioned the relevancy of, as we do. And I think he should be limited to maybe another five minutes to wrap up but I haven't seen from this cross-examination anything that would warrant an extensive extension of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please conclude in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, we've seen a number of references to Arkan, Zeljko Raznjatovic, including his presence at the video we reviewed and other references to him. First of all, we've -- this Court has already received evidence that Mr. Arkan -- Arkan claimed to have a very good relationship with you initially, what he termed as a brotherly relationship, that's D1612, but that it later turned into some form of conflict. Is that roughly accurate as you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say that that were different phases in our relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, back when the relationship was -- was still in the phase that Mr. -- that Arkan first refers to, that is the brotherly phase, Arkan went with you to Bosnia during the general period of the -- of Operation Corridor, right, at the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You've confused periods. First of all, we did not leave together, and we did not jointly participate in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there's a reference in a diary, a war diary, kept by the 1st Krajina Corps. The entry date is dated 26 July 1992. It states - and I'm happy to show it to you in a moment - General Ninkovic, commander of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence; Minister Milan Martic from the Serbian Republic of Krajina; General Borislav Djukic; and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, arrived at 1200 hours today. Does that refresh your recollection about Arkan coming with you or at least on the same day as you and the same time as you to the 1KK during the general period of the Corridor operation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the corridor was broken through, I returned on the 16th of July. I very well remember that. And as for the period that is discussed here, I believe it is not true. At least I can't remember that I was there, because this was at least ten days after Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly. 65 ter 15768, B/C/S page 127 and English page 123. Having the opportunity now to see the actual document and the reference to the -- by the way, just to clarify for the Court, General Dukic, he's -- was commander of the special understand of the RSK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but his name is not "Dukic," it is "Djukic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I mispronounced it. I see the slash on the D. Okay, so having had a chance to see that now does that refresh your recollection about the arrival of the 1KK at that time about those persons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember this event, and I really don't think I can see where this gathering was. I can't recall any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I guess we can't take it further in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document, Mr. President.
