utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection to this page being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On this item, whether it's only this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this item may go on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive these two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Martic, we heard the earlier references or saw the earlier references by Mr. Kostic to the various components of the special unit, and including volunteers, including DB members, including the RSK police. Mr. -- Arkan's -- Arkan and Arkan's forces worked together with the forces of the DB toward protecting the -- or toward what was considered to be protecting the Serbian areas of Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't put it that way, whether they worked together. As far as I know, Arkan did go to the battle-field, and he placed himself under the command of the one-time JNA, and then later either the VRS or our army of Srpska Krajina. So he placed himself under the command. Now that he was reassigned by the DB, I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know that, for example, that Arkan and his group were distributing weapons and ammunition and mines to, for example, the TO staffs and that that materiel was provided by the MUP and the Ministry of Defence of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- this is really the first time that I've heard that, that Arkan would distribute arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 01855. This is a document dated the 19th of October, 1991. It's an information report from the -- submitted to the first department of internal security of the SSNO, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and it refers to the activity of the Serbian volunteer -- Volunteers Guards, that is Arkan's unit, in the area of Erdut and it states in part: During several consecutive contacts with Arkan he stated that the weaponry, ammunition, and mines and explosives had been supplied by the MUP and the Ministry of the Defence of the Republic of Serbian and that he had been distributing them to the TO staffs in Erdut, Sarvas, and Borovo Selo. Records were being kept et cetera. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I object to the relevance of this. I think that this is now going into areas not related to the credibility of this witness and that touch upon things that you've excluded from this trial concerning arming of people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, that -- that -- if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is if it's necessary to respond and if the Court's interested in time and wants to move -- want to rule on, that's fine. But -- no -- that's the -- of course there's no independent interest here in what the Court has sought to exclude, that is, and had I wanted to get into the minutia of events and the details of events in Croatia for their own sake there would have been ample material to do so. This is not about the subject of arming in Croatia. This is about who Arkan was and who he was connected to, a matter of significant relevance to us in the context of the -- of events that took place in Bosnia. The Court is aware -- and in that regard, too, I mentioned -- I can also refer the Court to the fact that we've received evidence that Arkan's appearance in Zvornik was prompted by the intervention of a DB member and that's all I'll say about that and I can provide the Court with a citation to that. So it these -- this material that I'm covering now is extremely relevant and the attempt to find the context in which that issue is illuminated that sort of deflect it by characterising it as some effort in arming Croatia misses the point. The point is this is about who Arkan was, who he was connected to, and as the Court I'm sure considers relevant, how he ended up in Bosnia and what -- and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that this is still something that you have to draw a line somewhere, so I appreciate it's a difficult decision where to draw that line, but you could see that the relationship between Arkan and Bosnia changed over time, was different in 1992 than it was in 1994 and 1995, and so simply to say in 1991 that somewhere in Croatia he was taking arms from the Serbian MUP and distributing it to people I don't think really adds anything to the relevance to our case and goes, in my view, on the other side of the line that you've already drawn when you made the decision on Mr. Babic's testimony as to what would be relevant from Croatia and what would be not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view we can do without this document. Can you move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm moving on, by the way, to -- well, okay, I'll move on and see if it raises any other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, you referred to Golubic training centre, and it's correct, isn't it, that the first trainer at Golubic was Captain Dragan, the person we saw in the video?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, I should -- well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were aware, were you not, that it was the DB that recruited and sent him for that purpose; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to explain this because I was interrupted earlier. All of this follow upon the request of the president of the Executive Council of SAO Krajina, Mr. Babic. It was sent to President Milosevic and the Serbian MUP, a request to assist us with training our forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Understood. So if we could turn quickly to 65 ter 18775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, did you not hear the interpreter's intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. No, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, the interpretation staff indicated that they were unable to hear the last portion of your answer. What we received back was you said you had to explain. This followed the request of Mr. Babic: "It was sent to President Milosevic and the Serbian MUP, a request to assist us with training our forces." And they didn't hear anything thereafter. So if you had something additional, please indicate.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- in answer to the second part of your question that's correct, but it was my duty to say what ensued and what proceeded, and how it came about that Golubic was established, this training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in connection with that, I just want to quickly show you 65 ter 18775. This is a document dated the 8th of November, 1991. It's from Captain Dragan. He's expressing concern about what appears to be an effort to transform his status into reserve captain of the TO, stating the -- Captain Dragan has to remain Captain Dragan, and he explains that it's -- it was a -- it would be a risk to drown or merge him into the mass of reserve captains and he explains further: "I have the obligation toward the state security service of the Republic of Serbia and my activities within the TO have to be fully in accordance with the mentioned service." So I take it that that document is a reflection to essentially the same thing you referred to earlier that after seeking assistance from the MUP of Serbia they responded and now the person with whom they're responding is reflecting his obligation back toward the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to a request by Dr. Babic, Captain Dragan arrived. I believe he was brought by the DB people. Well, that second part we were not really interested in, but it was clear how it came about that he came. As for this document, what can I say about it? That's his dissatisfaction with his status, because previously he had been very present in the media and all of a sudden he disappeared from the media. So I have no idea what this is about. It does not necessarily mean, I don't really know, but it is possible that he did have some obligation toward the State Security Service of Serbia. I don't know about that. But I do know that when he was brought in, he was brought per our request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I don't think Mr. Martic has been able to confirm the parts of the document that Mr. Tieger wants him to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But this is not the time of document that requires that kind of contextual -- we've been through this before. This is a document of the type that is not previously required that kind of independent -- or affirmation like an interview or a newspaper article. So this is offered for purposes of -- I mean, whatever the witness says about it, he either affirms it or he says he doesn't know anything about it in the context of a statement in which he's offering opinions about the existence or nonexistence of a JCE. So it's relevant as impeachment for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Martic made sufficient comment for the purpose of admission in this case. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Martic, the last issue I wanted to take up with you arises from paragraph 19 of your statement, where you say that -- I'm sorry, paragraph 16 of your statement, where you assert that the JNA basically or for the most part severed as a buffer between Croatian and Serb positions. And then later in your statement, you go on to note that -- to discuss General Mladic and offer some positive words about his involvement in Croatia. Mr. Martic, the fact is that contrary to your assertion in your statement that the JNA served as a buffer, the fact is that, first, the Trial Chamber in your case found that the JNA only -- served as a buffer only until General Mladic arrived on the scene, and the fact is that you've stated that yourself previously; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you are skipping a lot of what had happened previously. The JNA was as buffer there in terms of separating our forces from the Croatian forces, but most importantly the beginning of the operation by the JNA, whatever preceded that and not what Babic said or other spin-masters who managed to pervert the facts and then use them against me and giving falsified facts in place of the real facts. There is an entire period when there were blockades of barracks and JNA garrisons where JNA soldiers were not only Serbs but also Croats and Muslims, Slovenes, people from all republics and of all ethnicities were put in a very difficult situation. They were killed. They were stopped from receiving the basic necessities: Water, food, electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And even to the point where --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you right now, because now you are doing what the Defence was asserting I was trying -- falsely asserting I was trying to do by concentrating on events in Croatia. I'm asking you this: Your statement indicates to this Chamber that the JNA served as a buffer. It talks positively about Ratko Mladic, and I'm saying to you that the reality is that you have admitted previously and I'll show you that in a moment, that until the time Mladic arrived the JNA served as a buffer and thereafter the JNA began functioning in offensive operations; right? That's what happened. Now, I know you want to provide all the reasons why that happened, but first can you acknowledge that that's true, that it was, that the JNA's role as a buffer was only until such time as Mladic came on the scene?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's exactly what I said, because as far as I know, Mladic arrived in late July or thereabouts in 1991. Now, when JNA for the first time clashed, was engaged in serious clashes, this was on the 26th of August, which is a month later. I would not put a stress on Mladic here because he was not the chief of that corps. I believe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last thing you said.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that at this time Mladic did not have a major role. He was not the commander of the Drina -- the Knin corps. Rather, I think he was the chief or the Chief of Operations, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you say now that's not -- that you wouldn't put the stress on that, but that's exactly what you did when you were interviewed earlier for a documentary. Let's turn to 65 ter 05263 at English page 10 and B/C/S page 10.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I was hoping to have the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you speak about General Mladic coming in June or July, creating a self-confidence to the Serbs, openly stating that the Serbs were right, and explicitly saying that until that moment the JNA and its officers were a buffer zone between us and Croatians. And although then a Colonel Mladic stated what other officers hadn't stated, that Serbs were right. So that was your position when you were interviewed here, Mr. Martic, correct, that General Mladic deserved the credit and his arrival deserved credit for changing what until that moment had been the role of the JNA as a buffer zone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can understand this, it is a distortion of my words, that I would credit Mladic with basically starting with the war where the conflict had been going on for a year before his arrival. When I was speaking about the JNA, I was speaking about the Knin corps and the way it was structured. Not a single man or person in a leading position in that corps was a Serb, and it was only with the arrival of Mladic that the Knin Corps had a Serb. So I'm not saying that with his arrival the situation practically changed and this does not reflect the truth, because for a good period of time he was a peacekeeper. He went to the other side and tried to make peace. That's true. Very nearly the clashes in Kijevo would happen, quite near to this period, and that was when the JNA practically got involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Martic. I tender this, and I appreciate the Court's additional time. That would be complete my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering about the format of this interview. This interview transcription does not include the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This particular -- no. That's -- it's a peculiarity of this. And I think we've used this in the past. This was from "The Death of Yugoslavia" series. Why it was transcribed in this way, I'm -- I'm not entirely certain, but that is an unfortunate byproduct of that particular transcription which is a transcription of lengthy tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's part of "Death of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my understanding Mr. President. I -- I can double-check. It's a very lengthy piece. I can check the -- two things, Mr. President. First of all, it -- it -- it is accurate, that is a portion of that interview conducted apparently on October 14th, 1994, and I should also add it was admitted as an exhibit, that is specifically Exhibit 496 in Mr. Martic's trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Martic, do you confirm that this is part of your interview? Although it might have been distorted, as you indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do agree with the part that it's disported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive this part.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Before you re-examine Mr. Martic, the Chamber is minded to give its ruling on the accused's motion for disclosure of records pertaining to Milan Babic filed by the accused on the 18th of March, 2013. The Chamber has reviewed the Deputy Registrar's fourth submission regarding medical records pertaining to Milan Babic filed on the 9th of May, 2013, as well as the ex parte annexes attached therein. These annexes contain inter alia the relevant medical information referred to in Judge Parker's report on Milan Babic's death. The Chamber notes that the said medical records, including inter alia the psychological evacuations conducted on the 5th of March, 2004, and the 7th of February, 2006, containing no suggestion that Milan Babic suffered from a personality disorder that would affect his credibility as a witness as was alleged by Milan Martic. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that the information provided by Judge Parker in his report on Milan Babic's death is a comprehensive account of the conclusions found in the medical reports and other information that the Chamber has reviewed. For those reasons, the Chamber is of the view that in the circumstances, the interest of justice does not demand that the accused be provided with the confidential medical information of Milan Babic. It has, therefore, decided to deny the accused 's motion for disclosure of Milan Babic's record. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, your Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, President Martic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to finish before the break. In that regard, I will ask you to provide me with short answers, if possible, if my questions are as concise as possible. You said a moment ago that the JNA got involved in the conflict at a point in time when it actually was confronted with the reasons to defend itself; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The issue concerned Captain Dragan. Before his arrival at the request of Milan Babic, was Captain Dragan convicted or even accused of a crime?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know what sort of relations existed between the state security of Serbia and the state security of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as I know, the two security services had some sort of animosity and mistrust prevailing between the two. Yugoslavia had been broken down, and there were still employees of other ethnicities working for the state security of Yugoslavia. So I couldn't call their relations harmonious, but they did co-operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which of the two security services was the one that Arkan was closer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the federal State Security Service. There are many documents which confirm the fact that he was practically there in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you happen to observe in whose official vehicles would Arkan come from the Republic of Serbia, which of the two security services?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the vehicles belonged to the federal service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the issue of Arkan, was Arkan captured by the Croatian side at some point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, and it was, I think, in late 1990. He spent roughly half a year in a prison in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Croatia bring him before a court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was never tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I know Mr. Karadzic is trying to move forward quickly. He's generally pretty good about reminding witnesses to pause so the translations can be made. That's not happening at the moment, so if both he and Mr. Martic could be reminded accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Please bear in mind. At least you should pause yourself, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully accept that, and I thank Mr. Tieger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the document P6313, the title of the document is "Report on the fulfillment of the obligation." Can you tell the Chamber whether there is any difference between the fulfillment of an obligation and execution of an order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the difference is enormous. One thing is the obligation that would arise from regulations, and that would boil down to one's day to day work. An order coming down from a superior institution is quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend the distinguished Mr. Tieger mentioned the joint criminal enterprise in connection with this document. Perisic asked that Celeketic let the convoy pass through. What is your understanding of the -- this event where a convoy was let through and the existence of a joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no joint criminal enterprise. That's a fictitious construct on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, I didn't introduce the document in the terms that Mr. Karadzic is suggesting. I asked about the document. It may be later on during the course of discussing the document's reference I was obliged to explain some aspects of its -- of how these issues interconnect, but that could not possibly in any event be a basis for inviting a dissertation by this witness on these matters, and I would ask that Mr. Karadzic be limited in redirect to factual issues specifically arising from the questions asked in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. Mr. Tieger didn't raise the issue of joint criminal enterprise with respect to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that may be correct, but in his cross-examination he raised the whole issue of who these people were working for and what the connection was between Milosevic and the people in Serbia and the other members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise. So I think that it comes within the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course, but connecting that to the document was inappropriate, in my opinion. Please, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just for what it's worth, if the accused wants to limit himself to asking questions about particular people that appear in a document or particular questions that were asked, that's one thing, but to fall back on some broad question of opinion calling for this breadth of legal and factual analysis akin to an expert is not appropriate and that's another one of the -- the flaws in this kind of approach and he adopted that approach in taking the statement. He wants to reintroduce it in the redirect inappropriately. And that's another thing -- I'm sorry to raise it but I'm just concerned it will come up in further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe that I'm right. When explaining the reasons why this document should be admitted, he mentioned joint criminal enterprise. There, I caught them in the act, that they were asking for the convoy to be let through. I mean, the latter part is my addition, but that is the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 23 of today's transcript, line 20, mention is made of the fact that Franko Simatovic, Frenki, said that the entire Serbian people was in jeopardy, was at risk. When was that special unit that was being discussed established, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The thing is that it was not meant to be established as a special unit. It was set up pursuant to a request from Milan Babic that people should be brought over to train our policemen for possible combat, which would come in handy since the conflict had basically begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the date of the 4th of May, 1991, that is mentioned, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It should be consistent roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in the document where Jovica Stanisic is mentioned, the neo-fascist elements in the Croatian government are mentioned. Can you tell us and you tried to do so during the cross-examination, what were the developments and what in these developments told you that a war was in the offing, and what does this word neo-Fascism that was mentioned by Simatovic tell you? What did this fact that he said that the entire Serbian people was at risk, what did that tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, this requires a broader explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course it does, and I'm going to object because it's the kind of question at best that can be posed to a witness in direct examination. It's very unlikely to arise from a cross-examination, and it didn't in this case. So to refer to some isolated reference in one of the documents that were put to the witness and then try to use that as a launching pad for a lengthy dissertation is inappropriate and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think the question was maybe -- quite a few elements in it, but if you take the one part where he refers to Mr. Simatovic saying that the entire Serbian people were at risk, this relates to something that was introduced during the cross-examination and I think Mr. Martic is allowed to explain what he believed Mr. Simatovic was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's easy for Mr. Robinson to say this was raised during cross-examination. I don't believe it was and I'd like him to explain how he considers this was raised by the cross-examination other than the fact that there are some documents that have peripheral references to this concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I thought that in the address Mr. Simatovic was making at the ceremony, the anniversary ceremony, that he had made some reference to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't consider that this topic arises out of the cross-examination. Even if it does, it would not assist the Chamber very much. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you were accused in the indictment and during the cross-examination it was said that you were a participant in the joint criminal enterprise together with me. I was allegedly a participant as well, which implied among other things the unification of the Serbian lands, the creation of a situation that would bring us all into one country, et cetera. What were the reasons for our communication? Did something prompt us to it, or was it completely out of the blue that we wanted to spoil an idyllic situation that prevailed in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest of terms, our ties were with a view to the preservation of Yugoslavia because we were in jeopardy with a neo-fascist government emerging in Croatia, and we were in the briefest of terms fighting for the preservation of Yugoslavia. Now as for the joint criminal enterprise alleged by the Prosecution, this is pure fiction. It's not something that ever existed. Or, to put it properly, there was a joint criminal enterprise on the part of the separatist forces that waged an armed conflict against Yugoslavia, and there is hard evidence to that effect. Both the presidents of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina publicly spoke out about it, that they wanted a war and that they could have averted a war had it been in their interest. So obviously in that quarter there was a joint criminal enterprise, but it was in somebody's interest to accuse us who were in favour of Yugoslavia of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You -- the charges accusing us that we wanted a common state. Did we ask for something that we had not had before or we already had a joint state.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already had a joint state in which all the peoples were equal and that included the Serbs, and we wanted the situation to remain as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the two presidents and their statements according to which they wanted a war, and what did you know about the activities and conduct of their closest associates? And as part of that conduct was there something that inspired you, prompted you to counteract?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Martic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, I object, sorry to do that, but clearly not arising from cross. In fact it arises from the witness's -- if it arises from anything, from the witness's answer to Dr. Karadzic's effort to re-introduce the subject after it had been previously and successfully objected to. But in any event, this is, you know, the activities of the associates of the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatia was not a matter that was raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My brief response to that would be this: The entire cross-examination suggested that the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia undertook unnecessary measures of caution or self-organisation. The organisation of events as if there hadn't been a reason for that, if there hadn't been a context. I would now like to ask President Martic to tell us what was behind that. Was that out of the blue that the Serbs provoked that, or was there a reason? The Prosecution painted a picture and portrayed Serbs as doing something with no good reason at all. And if you want me to be of assistance there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think your argument seems to be going too far. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, it's too broad. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case, it was suggested that units, instructors, Captain Dragan and others were sent to you. Why were they sent? Why did your units and MUP members have to be trained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of March, Croatian forces attacked us in Plitvice lakes. That was on the 31st of March. And one could say that that was the first serious incident that ever happened. After that, Milan Babic, who had already proclaimed himself as the president of the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina, decided to join that area to Serbia and that provoked rage, they in -- President Milosevic and others, because at that moment it was impossible to do that. That was not sustainable. After that there was a referendum, and the question for the referendum was whether you want to stay in Yugoslavia. The response was 100 per cent positive. The people opted for staying in Yugoslavia. After all that, Milan Babic did seek assistance. Actually, he requested help. He sent a request to Milosevic, the President of Serbia and the MUP of Serbia. He asked them to send people to train our own people for a possible war in the future, although there was already a war going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the leaders of Croatia even before that attack, do you remember Boljkovic, Spegelj, and others? Did they make any announcements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Things were going on. I would like to inform you about something else. Tudjman as the president of Croatia already in 1987 when he finally obtained a passport, although he could not have it before, he travelled to Canada and explained his plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was a bit misleading as well, but I'd like you to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I wanted to play a video-clip depicting Spegelj's words in the autumn of 1990 in preparation of war. With your permission, I would like to play it, and that was the foundation of everything that the Serbs did later in Croatia. And Spegelj was the minister of defence of Croat. Am I allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will hear from you, Mr. Tieger, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's an astonishingly - and I've said it before but I continue to feel that way - leading approach to even a bona fide attempt to introduce such a document explaining in advance how the witness should receive it. But beyond that, we're far afield from the questions posed on cross-examination. This is a continuing attempt by Mr. Karadzic to circumvent the Court's previous decisions about his effort to -- beyond the scope of direct and forces me to get on my feet repeatedly but I will continue to do so when he continues to ask questions that go beyond the scope, and this one clearly does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger's observation. If you have some other topics, shall we take a break? How long would you need, Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes or so. So perhaps a break would be welcome before I continue, or perhaps if you can allow me to go on for another ten minutes or so I can completely re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't have any difficulty with it, if it is convenient to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, you were asked about the opening of the corridor. Why was it necessary to open a corridor in a state? Why was it necessary to open that corridor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor was originally closed by the regular Croatian forces. There were a total of seven brigades that Tudjman had sent out to Posavina. Together with the Croatian forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Muslims, they closed the passage and cut off our Republic of Serbian Krajina, its western part and the Bosnian Krajina in its western part. People there were completely cut off from the state of Serbia. Not only were they cut off, but they were deprived of bare necessities, medicines. As a result, the situation became extremely difficult. People who were sick were dying because of the shortage of medicine. There was the notorious case of the 12 babies who died in Banja Luka because of the lack of oxygen. In Knin, people on dialysis were dying. So it was a tacit murder of those of person. Before that, we sent hundreds of letters to the United Nations, the Secretary-General, the presiding of the Security Council, and two various other addressees asking them to allow us to get our supplies from Serbia because the situation was simply unbearable. It was simply unbelievable that we were a territory under the protection of the United Nations and we were still reduced to such a position. One of those attempts was our agreement in Banja Luka. What I remember, President Karadzic, is something that is branded in my memory. After all the possible attempts of correspondence and sending letters to various addresses, you still tried to convince the international community, at least that's what you told us, to give us the so-called blue road, which means that our convoys with medicines and food would be escorted by the United Nations. Unfortunately, that was all fruitless, but I remember how much you tried to deal with matters in a peaceful way. And after that, the only possible solution was to break the corridor through by force otherwise we would have died. The whole region was condemned to starvation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, President. I will move on to another topic. Let's avoid confusion. You said the seven brigades of the Croatian Army. You were talking about a corridor that was close. Was it in Croatia or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Bosnian Posavina, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the possible unification or the possible creation or preservation of Yugoslavia or the creation of an alliance of Serbian states, and so on and so forth. Did I or you or anybody else who was mentioned in the indictment show preparedness to sacrifice peace for any goal whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the answer is yes. I remember that beared very well. We even made concessions in order to establish peace. All the options that were part of your activities were geared towards peace. One thing that I cannot forget is your effort to have everybody accept Vance's plan. Among many people, members of the academia, and wise people in Serbia who opted for Vance's plan and peacekeeping forces that would be a protective force in Croatia, and that all would result in a political solution. You advocated that and that was accepted. Another striking moment in your activity was when you worked in favour of Cutileiro's plan, although it was not in favour of us, but even at our own detriment you accepted that. So even at our own detriment we did our best to find a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: President, the first sentence on line 5, does this mean that we were prepared to sacrifice peace for our own goals, or did we want to deal with matters peacefully? The way it was recorded is that we were prepared to sacrifice peace.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I may have misspoken. It was just the contrary. We were in favour of peace, which is why we were prepared to do things that are our own detriment at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In P2555 which is a document that I would like to call up for a brief moment, this is my correspondence with Vukovic and Grahovac. It's a P document, 2555, page 3. It's a Prosecution document. Page 3, please. Let's look at the biggest entry in the middle. Radovan Karadzic is speaking, and he says we want to stay in the federal state of Yugoslavia. Do you want to be a Greater Serbia or a separate republic? A separate republic is the best, an unrealistic option for Milan to us for a separate federal unit. How does this tally with your information about my activities and what I advocated? How does this tally with my effort to preserve Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see this is what happened after the Grahovo declaration, if I'm not mistaken. You are talking to Mr. Vukic, and you explain to him what would happen if Babic's option had been accepted. The option for us to ask to be in the federation as a new federation member corresponds to the peaceful solution of the crisis, but obviously it was impossible to form an association that would include Bosnian Krajina, predominantly inhabited by the Serbs, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I believe that this is what you're talking about. This is your interpretation as to what would happen if things remained as they were. You were in favour of a federal unit rather than the proposal tabled by Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You pointed out that you knew that I advocated constitutional solutions. In your view did the course of developments impose changes to our positions? Before the war broke out and after the war broke out, did our positions remain the same? Could they remain the same?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MARTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they had to change with the situation. However, in all the combinations, as far as I knew you, you always advocated peaceful options and solutions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, President. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Martic. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. And I -- the Chamber's thanks also go to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I hope that the DU knows about your decision that it concerns also President Martic, that I can meet him after the -- his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber made it clear when it gave its clarification on order earlier on. Before we have a break, I have a question for Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson. I am take it that Mr. Borovcanin has already arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the -- under the anticipation that he would give testimony last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When he is going to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the first week of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the Chamber fully understand the difficulty related to the logistics and the unexpected delay as in the case of Mr. Galic's testimony, the Chamber is concerned about the unnecessary prolongation of the stay of the detained witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The reason for Mr. Borovcanin's scheduling is twofold. First you imposed a 14-day notice requirement so that his testimony cannot commence until 14 days after his statement is disclosed. And secondly, we had scheduled his testimony for the end of May, but at the request of the Prosecution we postponed it until early June because of the unavailability of the lawyer who was to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the moment I leave it at that, but please bear in mind that in the general sense the Chamber has concerns such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before we continue, as regards the Special Police celebration video-clip, the Chamber will add only those parts, excerpts shown to the witness, to the existing evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think just by way of quick clarification, Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that means the portions also read out to him, it's not physically showing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, physically shown. Shown parts. We didn't hear anything about --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's address it when we have a moment to do so and I'll get the portions I'm referring to, but I advised him that the transcript contained references. I hoped that transcript would be called up, and so on, but it was intended to be the precise equivalent of showing it in any other form. I mean, it was intended to cover -- to confront the witness with the portion, the relevant portion of the video and the transcript indicate precisely what the substance of that was and in fact what it was verbatim, and then ask questions about that. So I -- I'm simply hoping that the fact that the video real wasn't shown should not preclude those portions from being admitted in. In this case to the best of my recollection, it's only the final faze of a lengthy speech, most of which is already in evidence, so for expediency I simply identified the portion that wasn't. And one reference to one sentence, homage, that was paid to somebody else. That's my recollection of what it included, but I would hope that that wouldn't preclude the admission of those portions because it's simply a different modality but the same substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without being asked general questions, all Mr. Martic did was a confirmation of certain identification of a few individuals. So I think in liaising with the parties, the court deputy would be able to identify the portion put to the witness. That's the ruling. Good afternoon, Dr. Subotic. Do you hear in me your language, Dr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that your viral infection is a bit worse than it was during proofing. So if at any point in time you need a break, please let us know and I'm sure that the Trial Chamber will take due action.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said in the proofing room that I have a problem with my throat, but I hope that won't be a problem and I will be able to complete my testimony. I do have a request. During the proofing, I realised that there were a certain number of errors in my report that might lead to a misunderstanding or to a poor understanding of the subject matter, so I would like to point them out now before we begin, because there was no occasion to enter these corrections into my report before I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have to request, and I will have to remind myself, too, that you pause between my question and your answer, and I should do the same, and sometimes the interpretation will lag behind. Now, as for the corrections, I will ask you when we reach that point in the report. I will ask you about what it is you want to correct, but before that, could you tell us briefly, because the Trial Chamber have before them your CV and your bibliography, so would you just briefly tell us about your background, your expertise, the posts that you occupied, the work that you did, the jobs, the number of reports or works that you did, and so on. Could you just give us a brief outline of your background.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I completed the University of Belgrade school of mechanical engineering. That's how I began my career. And after I earned my bachelors degree, I began working for the Military Technical Institute in the classical weapons section --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Conventional weapons, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the ballistics subsection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many expert papers did you write or draft?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe over 100, perhaps 120 to 150. And these research papers were -- they differed. There are papers that were published after national an international conventions and congresses, and also the research I did as part of my work at the Military Technical Institute. In addition, since 2000 or -- since the year 2000, I have been an expert witness for ballistics registered with the Ministry of Justice in the Republic of Serbia, and I was re-appointed two years ago. And I also work on developing designs for warehouses and ranges, shooting ranges, for training purposes for firearms, as well as design of warehouses for storing ammunition and lethal assets both for military purposes and for civilian use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Dr. Subotic, although Mr. Karadzic advised you, I would like to advise you again. In particular, we -- since we are going to deal with very technical issues, it's imperative for you to put a pause before you start answering the question. Probably you will be familiar with watching the LiveNote transcription from time to time, so when interpretation of Mr. Karadzic's question is concluded, it is then time for you to start answering the question. If you could pay attention to that, please. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I thought that I was already minding it, and I will be very careful. My apologies once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that due to the speed of speech there may have been a misunderstanding. Did you say that you design warehouses and shooting ranges or only warehouses?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I said that I design shooting ranges and warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to interpret a shooting range. Perhaps it's better to say shooting polygons, I'm not sure, but anyhow, these are ranges where shooting is conducted; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in other projects? Is there anything else in your professional resume that you would like to point out as a dominant feature of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if there's anything else I should add to this resume that I've already handed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please take a look at your expertise on modified aerial bombs. Could you please give us a brief summary of the report. Tell us who drafted it and what it comprised.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I will first answer your question and then I will take this opportunity to make the corrections that you said I may do when the document in question is before us. I prepared my paper together with my associates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt at this stage. Two things. The witness appears to be referring to a document that is apparently not her report, a document she has in front of her, I'm sorry, and if we could just get some indication of what that is and what the references are. Two, she's now mentioned a couple of times corrections that it appears Dr. Karadzic is familiar with she wishes to make to her report, corrections that arose in proofing. We have received no notice of any corrections, so I'd just like to get some clarification as to why that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Robinson could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I myself was not aware of corrections, so I think Dr. Karadzic will have to address that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just learned about this just before we began, and I believe these are really typographical errors and minor details to deal with technical parameters and figures perhaps, but there's nothing of a substantial nature. These are just minor errors that Dr. Subotic noticed during the proofing. During the proofing we did not make those corrections, but we will see what it is about when she points them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't learned this during the proofing. The transcript does not reflect what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. What doctor said is this: "During the proofing, I realised that there were a certain number of errors in my report that might lead to a misunderstanding or a poor understanding." So it arose during the proofing process, didn't it? Dr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. This happened during my final preparations for this testimony, and I noted it down, and I stressed it. I pointed it out here because I felt that I should do so, and I brought these corrections with me here, but we did not really have an opportunity -- I did not have an opportunity to give them to anyone because I've just arrived recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what you have in front of you is those corrections? So are you satisfied with the clarification, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me, but I'll leave it at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe there's a misunderstanding, because Dr. Subotic said that this happened during her preparations and not during our co-operation. Her preparations on her own. Now, could you please tell us what these corrections are, what pages they should be on, and we will begin with the modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. On page 64, the last two lines in the text on this page read in parentheses, "On condition that these were --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, because the pages differ in English and in Serbian, would you please refer to paragraph numbers. Perhaps that's better. Would this be in paragraph 30?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, that's paragraph 30. The fifth paragraph from the top. So it reads, "On the condition that these were FAB 250/4," and it should read instead "On the condition that these were FAB 250/4 or 250/3."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please go on. Now, could you just tell us what these /3 and /4 are a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following. Did you locate the paragraph, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. In the copy I have it's at the bottom of page 66, some language that's in parentheses, two lines up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the problem seems to be that we have various versions of the report. Shall we upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then pull up in e-court -- just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the paragraph numbers would be the same in any version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 30 in my version begins with "Berko Zecevic," whereas paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from the aforementioned, it is clear that -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit number -- or the 65 ter number for the air-bomb report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that's 1D25159. We have a redacted version, so I'm not really sure. 7900. That's 65 ter 1D7900.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think in that 65 ter it is again at the bottom of page 66, in the English at least.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So can we see paragraph 30. That would be between the pages 64 and 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In my hard copy version, paragraph 30 appears on page 69. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian we see it now, and those are the last two lines where this correction has to be made. Could we see page 30 in English. Yes, now, we have it. And here it is the last three lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we should add either FAB or FAB-250/3. Could you tell us what this is a reference to, FAB-250/3?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This designation FAB-250/4 and FAB-250/3 means that this is a modified aerial bomb because two or three rocket engines were modified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Three or four.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the next correction is?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the same document, the next correction concerns paragraph 47, which in my copy is page 72, line 3, where it reads, "As stated in item --" actually, it reads under item 32, "As stated in item 45."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English it does seem to say item 45.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, then it must be a correction that I notified you of earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you direct your attention to line 3 in paragraph 47 in the English version. Is that the correction you meant? You also have the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I must have sent this correction out previously and then noticed it unchanged in my own copy. Anyway, also, paragraph 61 in my copy, that's page 94 paragraph 2, line 1, below image 42, it reads: "For the projectile in image 41," whereas it should read "The projectile from image 42." There's one other correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us with what we have on our screens? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I meant image or figure 42. That should be on the next page, because we need figure 42.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 93 on the screen, and I need page 94 in Serbian. Yes. There it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: English next page, please, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the line in question?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the page in Serbian. It's paragraph 2 below figure 42 where it reads: "For the projectile in figure 41," whereas it should read "figure 42" instead of "figure 41."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we find it in English, please? It's the second or the third paragraph in English. You see it, the projectile in figure [In English] 60. It goes to the figure -- "Projectile in figure 41." It should be "42." [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you give us the next correction?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: There is another correction which relates to paragraph 64. Under C in my copy it's page 96.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 103 is the page in English. 103, 103 English, C.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Sub-item C, line 3, reads -- actually, line 2, "Aerial bomb FAB-100 with one or three motors or engines," whereas it should read the "FAB-100 aerial bomb with three engines," as is in fact the case. And that will be all for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the word "one," or rather, the bit "one or" should be deleted?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and only "three" should stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And those would be all the corrections you had in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now briefly go through the incidents. Can you introduce them to us, and then if need be, we will go into more detailed explanations. Look at incident G10, please. It is an incident at Hrasnica near the Aleksa Santic school. Can you tell us in a nutshell what sort of physical evidence you had and what were your conclusions based on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: As was the case with all the other incidents, in this one, too, we used the documents that contained the following information: They were either the investigation documents belonging to the local police, investigation documents belonging to UNPROFOR and KDZ, documents which were witness statements or testimonies, footage which related to these incidents, as well as all the various documents that we were able to obtain from the previous trials which looked into these incidents. As for this specific incident, based on the physical traces that could be obtained from the site we arrived at the conclusion about the type of bomb, the incoming trajectory or the direction from which it came, and the possible target. We established what the type and form of bomb. Now, the type of bomb, based on the material evidence contained in CSB documents, and based on the information that could be gleaned from the photographs of the feature that was hit, and on the basis of the destructive power that could be ascertained based on these photographs, it was concluded that this was the result of a FAB-100 with a TNT charge, that the incoming trajectory, based on the diagram of the scene, which was also provided, passed across the Aleksa Santic school. Based on the video footage, it was established that this was a military feature which was mentioned in this report, and in particular it was established that this was not a bomb that would have spatial effect because there are survivors, live witnesses who would not have survived in that particular incident had the bomb been of spatial effect. Another thing that I have to say is there was a FAB-100 with three rocket engines of the Grad type, and that it impacted upon contact with the building, which is something that was concluded by the investigators of UNPROFOR. I think it was captain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and this, too, can be deduced from the facts that the projectile made where the damage was such that -- that the building caved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that this was an area bomb, can you tell us what the charges of one bomb and what the charges of the other bomb would be?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: When I say that this is an area bomb, I mean that it was filled with liquid explosive, the so-called fuel air explosive, and I think that my collaborator Dr. Andjelkovic explained this in greater detail, but let me explain it briefly. This is the principle according to which this bomb works: It consists of a single container wherein there is liquid explosive. There is a small solid explosive charge whose only purpose is to break open the container. Once the liquid explosive spills out, it mixes with oxygen, thus bringing into play the primers under pressure of between 20 to 40 bars that would be active in an area of between 20 to 40 metres. The main purpose of this bomb would be to clear an area of mines. However, this bomb proved highly effective in combat against living organisms, and the effect of such a bomb is highly lethal, and as a rule, any living organism in the area will die.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you find it important to state that this was not a fuel air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason behind it was that in my colleague Berko Zecevic, in his expert report that was presented here in this case claimed the opposite, in fact; namely that the fuel air-bomb was at play here, and we had to analyse the effects upon the target and to check how founded this assertion was from a highly technical point of view. I forgot to mention that as I said at the very beginning, there is a quantity of between 2 to 3 kilogrammes of liquid explosives. The containers that are broken open remain in large fragments, and in none of these cases were the investigators able to find large fragments of the jacket which would be one of the serious reasons to suspect that there was an area bomb at play at that scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we briefly look at paragraph 10 and figure 9. You said that the bomb flew along its trajectory above the Aleksa Santic school. And how far was it from the Aleksa Santic school that the bomb landed?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We visited the scene of the incident, as is know, and the school -- or, rather, the fence of the school is 20 metres away from the building that was hit. The school itself was some 17 to 18 metres away. We didn't really measure the distance. It was inappropriate to go there when the school pupils were there. So we measured the distance between the fence and the building, and it was found to be 20 metres, whereas the report itself said that it was between 70 and 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what does figure 9 depict? And we can leave only the English version on the screen for the time being.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Figure 9 depicts a sketch of the site which was drafted by the investigator. From the crater you can see the trajectory of the bomb, and that trajectory, trajectory 1 which was established by the CVS Sarajevo, when that trajectory is transposed onto Google Earth map, it runs parallelly, and if you tie this to the place of the incident you can see that it goes right above the Aleksa Santic school. That's why we concluded, and also based on the fact that it was very close to the school, i.e., that it was less than 0.5 probable radial aberrations, that the target was most probably the Aleksa Santic school, because on the site of the military school it was seen that -- it was also a military facility, i.e., that military training was taking place there which is what you can find in our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you cannot calculate, can you then just assume what was the overshoot in respect of the school? The bomb flew across the roof; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, we did not do that calculation. It can be calculated. The overshoot was very minute in terms of the height. I really can't tell you how much, but I suppose it was less than 1 metre across the roof or over the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have the time, but let me just say that you did not see a new United Nations document dated the 9th February, and in that document it is stated that that was probably retaliation for a mortar shell that had landed a minute or two before that bomb. But it is really not necessary to deal with the ballistics of that. However, if you'd seen that report, I suppose that it would have been easier for you to make your conclusions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, same thing. It doesn't appear to have been a question, just useless commentary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I had the time, I would display the document, but I don't. If that document had been disclosed earlier, I'm sure that Dr. Subotic would have added and would have taken it into account. Let's look at G11 and tell us, please, briefly, what that was about. In my copy it's page 57. In English it must be thereabouts. Paragraph 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to take a look. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have paragraph 14. Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is physical evidence and what did it show with regard to this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The incident occurred in Safeta Zajke Street 43. A bomb landed in the street. Everything is very well marked here, and we had very good traces. Obviously there were certain discrepancies with regard to the findings based on documents. I will draw your attention to the fact that we concluded based on the effects on the target that that was a bomb FAB-100 with three engines. It was absolutely impossible for a bomb like that, an area bomb, to create a crater of the kind as can be seen in photos. It is impossible that something like that would happen. An area bomb contains 3 kilos explosives, so a crater should be small. And we also saw the craters that are produced by 120-millimetre shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at paragraph 25, figure 15, and can you explain the conclusions of previous investigations about the incoming trajectory. Paragraph 25 in -- and figure 15.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have three trajectories, strategic south which was determined by the CSBs, marked by 1; the azimuth 155 trajectory as determined by Mr. Zecevic. He did not investigate. He made his conclusion based on the drawing and the azimuth 146 azimuth trajectory which was determined by the defence expert based on the schematic. You can see it in figure 14. You can see how we did that. That figure shows that we overlapped the image of the street with a street plan and then we drew our conclusions based on the position of the crater, and that's how we were able to determine the trajectory of the bomb. As I've already told you, here again there was a confusion with regard to the claim that the bomb was an area bomb. From the technical parameter, we can see that that was impossible, because a crater of these dimensions could not have been created by an area bomb. On the other hand, it was not a 250 bomb. Again, dimensions of the crater would not correspond to such a bomb. We carried out investigations, and we documented that in that case. The crater would have been of much bigger dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me just say that all these three trajectories, the one determined by us, by the CSB, and by Mr. Zecevic, they all overshot the wire factory, which is why we concluded that it could have been the target. And that factory was used in war production, at least according to our information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what building would that be in this photo or on -- in this figure before we go back to figure 14. Can you look at the figure on the screen. Can you point us to the building.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The building is actually at the point where all these lines meet. Actually, the bomb did not land on the building itself but on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far from the building?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: How far from the building? Let me see how far from the building it landed. The place where the bomb landed was about 100 metres from the wire factory. I have to say immediately that the distance of 100 metres or so is within the range of one radial aberration. And let me say immediately that we took into account the average distance from the place from which the bomb was fired to the place where it landed as being 6 kilometres, because the exact parameters did not exist to tell us what the place of launch was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the participants, when you say one or two or three radial aberrations, what measure is that, or radial deviation?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I'll try and explain it in simple terms. Actually we're talking about a statistical description of the probability of the realisation of an event or a statistical bias. When it comes to this kind of a physical phenomenon, we use -- or, rather, the physical process behaves in accordance with the Gauss distribution. According to that we have areas within which certain events take place. Some of them with the certainty of 50 per cent or 70 per cent, 90 per cent, or 100 per cent. When I say 1VV which stands for one probable radial deviation, that means that within the range of 2 radial deviations there are 50 per cent of probable realisations of a certain event. Within the range of 4, i.e., plus/minus 2 we can find 75 per cent, plus minus three is 90 per cent and 4 is the margin of the area where these events --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean the left or the right extreme?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It seems that I was too fast. So the remaining few percentage points is where we are talking. The reminder up to the 100 per cent which us ballistic experts consider to be inadmissible deviation when it comes to the probability of hitting a target. I don't know whether I've been clear enough, but I've tried to explain the bell curve as best as I could in simple terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the hypothesis as to how big was the overshoot in terms of the height of the building?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you how big the overshoot was but say that descent angles were small. We can apply simple trigonometry and we can determine how far it was because we're talking about a distance of no more than 100 metres. Those angles are relatively small, not bigger than 25 degrees. I can't tell you off the cuff how much it was and I wouldn't be able to do even the simplest calculation without a calculator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I draw your attention to incident G12. I believe that you said 20 degrees, not 90.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was 20, not 90. I'm sorry, I'm not following the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it was also said that you can't do it off the cuff without a calculator; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at G12 and tell us what this is all about? What was the physical evidence there, and what did it allow you to conclude?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The physical evidence here, we can see the sketch of the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at paragraph 32. I apologise. And figure 16. Perhaps it's on the following page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Here we have Majdanska Street with no number. This was a modified aerial bomb which impacted next to the transformer station.
